501|[![Two lines of warships at sea sailing with full sails downwind away from the viewer and firing broadsides at one another; in the center foreground receding into the left background, six of the French fleet; in the right foreground receding to the center four of the British fleet.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/BattleOfVirginiaCapes.jpg/250px-BattleOfVirginiaCapes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BattleOfVirginiaCapes.jpg)
502|
503|A [French Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Navy "French Navy") fleet (left) engages the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") in the [Battle of the Chesapeake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Chesapeake "Battle of the Chesapeake") on September 5, 1781
504|
505| [![Center foreground a British officer on the left standing surrenders to a mounted Continental officer; far left foreground receding into the center background, a British line of infantry then mounted cavalry, with a large white flag of surrender; far right foreground receding into the center background, a Continental line of infantry, then mounted cavalry, with a large US flag of the Army.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Surrender_of_Lord_Cornwallis.jpg/250px-Surrender_of_Lord_Cornwallis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Surrender_of_Lord_Cornwallis.jpg)
506|
507|British general [Cornwallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Cornwallis,_1st_Marquess_Cornwallis "Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis") surrenders at [Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown "Siege of Yorktown") in October 1781
508|
509|Clinton spent most of 1781 based in New York City; he failed to construct a coherent operational strategy, partly due to his difficult relationship with Admiral [Marriot Arbuthnot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriot_Arbuthnot "Marriot Arbuthnot").[[250]](#cite_note-ap5wX-280) In [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina"), Cornwallis independently developed an aggressive plan for a campaign in Virginia, which he hoped would isolate Greene's army in the [Carolinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinas "Carolinas") and cause the collapse of Patriot resistance in the [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"). This strategy was approved by Lord Germain in London, but neither informed Clinton.[[251]](#cite_note-mnb58-281)
510|
511|Washington and [Rochambeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Donatien_de_Vimeur,_comte_de_Rochambeau "Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau") discussed their options: Washington wanted to attack the British in New York, and Rochambeau wanted to attack them in [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), where Cornwallis's forces were less established.[[252]](#cite_note-xzQbp-282) Washington eventually gave way, and Lafayette took a combined Franco-American force into Virginia.[[253]](#cite_note-bsnMy-283) Clinton misinterpreted his movements as preparations for an attack on New York and instructed Cornwallis to establish a fortified sea base, where the Royal Navy could evacuate British troops to help defend New York.[[254]](#cite_note-b3QwE-284)
512|
513|When Lafayette entered Virginia, Cornwallis complied with Clinton's orders and withdrew to [Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown,_Virginia "Yorktown, Virginia"), where he constructed strong defenses and awaited evacuation.[[255]](#cite_note-SkAo5-285) An agreement by the [Spanish Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Navy "Spanish Navy") to defend the French West Indies allowed Admiral [François Joseph Paul de Grasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Joseph_Paul_de_Grasse "François Joseph Paul de Grasse") to relocate to the Atlantic seaboard, a move Arbuthnot did not anticipate.[[250]](#cite_note-ap5wX-280) This provided Lafayette naval support, while the failure of previous combined operations at [Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_News,_Virginia "Newport News, Virginia") and [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia") meant their coordination was planned more carefully.[[256]](#cite_note-6XKWu-286) Despite repeated urging from his subordinates, Cornwallis made no attempt to engage Lafayette before he could establish siege lines.[[257]](#cite_note-jzAf8-287) Expecting to be withdrawn within a few days, he also abandoned the outer defenses, which were promptly occupied by the besiegers and hastened British defeat.[[258]](#cite_note-4QJnx-288)
514|
515|On August 31, a Royal Navy fleet under [Thomas Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Graves,_1st_Baron_Graves "Thomas Graves, 1st Baron Graves") left New York for Yorktown.[[259]](#cite_note-xdltf-289) After landing troops and munitions for the besiegers on August 30, de Grasse remained in Chesapeake Bay and intercepted him on September 5; although the [Battle of the Chesapeake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Chesapeake "Battle of the Chesapeake") was indecisive in terms of losses, Graves was forced to retreat, leaving Cornwallis isolated.[[260]](#cite_note-pTsmW-290) An attempted breakout over the [York River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_River_(Virginia) "York River (Virginia)") at [Gloucester Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester_County,_Virginia#Gloucester_County_formation_and_divisions "Gloucester County, Virginia") failed due to bad weather.[[261]](#cite_note-0d9W7-291) Under heavy bombardment with dwindling supplies, on October 16 Cornwallis sent emissaries to General Washington to negotiate surrender; after twelve hours of negotiations, the terms of surrender were finalized the following day.[[262]](#cite_note-g66wL-292) Responsibility for defeat was the subject of fierce public debate between Cornwallis, Clinton, and Germain. Clinton ultimately took most of the blame and spent the rest of his life in relative obscurity.[[263]](#cite_note-irWjD-293)
516|
517|Subsequent to Yorktown, American forces were assigned to supervise the armistice between Washington and Clinton made to facilitate British departure following the January 1782 law of Parliament forbidding any further British offensive action in North America. British-American negotiations in Paris led to signed preliminary agreements in November 1782, which acknowledged US independence. The enacted [Congressional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") war objective, a British withdrawal from North America and cession of these regions to the US, was completed in stages in East Coast cities.[[264]](#cite_note-OtLkf-294)
518|
519|In the US South, Generals Greene and Wayne observed the British removing their troops from Charleston on December 14, 1782.[[265]](#cite_note-FF82B-295) Loyalist provincial militias of whites and free Blacks and Loyalists with slaves were transported to Nova Scotia and the British West Indies.[[ae]](#cite_note-296) Native American allies of the British and some freed Blacks were left to escape unaided through the American lines.
520|
521|On April 9, 1783, Washington issued orders that "all acts of hostility" were to cease immediately. That same day, by arrangement with Washington, Carleton issued a similar order to British troops.[[266]](#cite_note-zaInj-297) As directed by a Congressional resolution of May 26, 1783, all non-commissioned officers and enlisted were furloughed "to their homes" until the "definitive treaty of peace", when they would be automatically discharged. The US armies were directly disbanded in the field as of Washington's General Orders on June 2, 1783.[[267]](#cite_note-clMCt-298) Once the Treaty of Paris was signed with Britain on September 3, 1783, Washington resigned as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.[[264]](#cite_note-OtLkf-294) The last British occupation of New York City ended on November 25, 1783, with the departure of Clinton's replacement, General Sir [Guy Carleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Carleton,_1st_Baron_Dorchester "Guy Carleton, 1st Baron Dorchester").[[268]](#cite_note-Xx5DW-299)
522|
523|## Strategy and commanders
524|
525|[![West Point Military Academy MAP of America east of the Mississippi River. Campaigns noted in New England; in the middle colonies with three British (red sailing ship) naval victories; in the South with two British naval victories, and in Virginia with one French (blue sailing ship) naval victory. A Timeline bar graph below shows almost all British (red bar) victories on the left in the first half of the war, and almost all US (blue bar) victories on the right in the second half of the war.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/USMA01_Major_Campaigns_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War.jpg/250px-USMA01_Major_Campaigns_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:USMA01_Major_Campaigns_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War.jpg)
526|
527|A map of principal campaigns in the American Revolutionary War[[269]](#cite_note-BTKUJ-300) with British movements in red and American movements in blue; the timeline shows the British won most battles in the war's first half, but Americans won the most in the second.
528|
529|To win their insurrection, Washington and the Continental Army needed to outlast the British will to fight. To restore [British America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_America "British America"), the British had to defeat the Continental Army quickly and compel the Second Continental Congress to retract its claim to self-governance.[[270]](#cite_note-I7Xou-301) Historian Terry M. Mays of [The Citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Citadel "The Citadel") identifies three separate types of warfare during the Revolutionary War. The first was a colonial conflict in which objections to imperial trade regulation were as significant as taxation policy. The second was a civil war between American Patriots, American Loyalists, and those who preferred to remain neutral. Particularly in the south, many battles were fought between Patriots and Loyalists with no British involvement, leading to divisions that continued after independence was achieved.[[271]](#cite_note-StQAE-302)
530|
531|The third element was a global war between France, [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Spain "Kingdom of Spain"), the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic"), and Britain, with America serving as one of several different war theaters.[[271]](#cite_note-StQAE-302) After entering the Revolutionary War in 1778, France provided the Americans money, weapons, soldiers, and naval assistance, while French troops fought under US command in North America. While Spain did not formally join the war in America, they provided access to the Mississippi River and captured British possessions on the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") that denied bases to the Royal Navy, [retook Menorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Minorca_(1781) "Invasion of Minorca (1781)") and [besieged Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Siege_of_Gibraltar "Great Siege of Gibraltar") in Europe.[[272]](#cite_note-ONzWM-303) Although the Dutch Republic was no longer a major power prior to 1774, they still dominated the European carrying trade, and Dutch merchants made large profits by shipping French-supplied munitions to the Patriots. This ended when Britain declared war in December 1780, and the conflict proved disastrous to the Dutch economy.[[273]](#cite_note-72JXk-304)
532|
533|### American strategy
534|
535|The Americans stood to benefit if the Continental Army remained intact and the armed conflict became a protracted war. British supply lines were long, replacement of troops difficult, and the war was expensive. Colonial populations were largely prosperous and depended on local production for food and supplies rather than on imports from Britain. The thirteen colonies were spread across most of North American Atlantic seaboard, stretching 1,000 miles. Most colonial farms were remote from the seaports, and control of four or five major ports did not give Britain control over American inland areas. Each state had established internal distribution systems.[[274]](#cite_note-lNS5K-305) Motivation was also a major asset: each colonial capital had its [own newspapers and printers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_American_publishers_and_printers "Early American publishers and printers"), and the Patriots enjoyed more popular support than the Loyalists. Britain hoped that the Loyalists would do much of the fighting, but found that the Loyalists did not engage as significantly as they had hoped.[[13]](#cite_note-6bqxv-24)
536|
537|#### Continental Army
538|
539|Main article: [Continental Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army")
540|
541|See also: [Militia (United States) § American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militia_(United_States)#American_Revolutionary_War_(1775–1783) "Militia (United States)"), and [Minutemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minutemen "Minutemen")
542|
543|[![Formal painting of General George Washington, standing in uniform, as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/George_Washington%2C_1776.jpg/250px-George_Washington%2C_1776.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Washington,_1776.jpg)
544|
545|1776 portrait of [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") by [Charles Willson Peale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Willson_Peale "Charles Willson Peale"), now housed in the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum")
546|
547|When the Revolutionary War began, the Second Continental Congress lacked a professional army or navy. However, each of the colonies had a long-established system of local militia, which were combat-tested in support of British regulars in the French and Indian War. The colonial state legislatures independently funded and controlled their local militias.[[274]](#cite_note-lNS5K-305)
548|
549|Militiamen were lightly armed, had little training, and usually did not have uniforms. Their units served for only a few weeks or months at a time and lacked the training and discipline of more experienced soldiers. Local county militias were reluctant to travel far from home and were unavailable for extended operations.[[275]](#cite_note-JOPiQ-306) To compensate for this, the Continental Congress established a regular force known as the Continental Army on June 14, 1775, which proved to be the origin of the modern [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), and appointed Washington as its commander-in-chief. However, it suffered significantly from the lack of an effective training program and from largely inexperienced officers.[[276]](#cite_note-4DbAi-307) Each state legislature appointed officers for both county and state militias and their regimental Continental line officers; although Washington was required to accept Congressional appointments, he was permitted to choose and command his own generals, such as Greene; his chief of artillery, Knox; and [Alexander Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton"), the chief of staff.[[277]](#cite_note-pSJBj-308) One of Washington's most successful general officer recruits was Steuben, a veteran of the Prussian general staff who wrote the [Revolutionary War Drill Manual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_War_Drill_Manual "Revolutionary War Drill Manual").[[276]](#cite_note-4DbAi-307) The development of the Continental Army was always a work in progress and Washington used both his regulars and state militias throughout the war; when properly employed, the combination allowed them to overwhelm smaller British forces, as they did in battles at Concord, Boston, Bennington, and Saratoga. Both sides used partisan warfare, but the state militias effectively suppressed Loyalist activity when British regulars were not in the area.[[27... [truncated]
550|
551|Washington designed the overall military strategy in cooperation with Congress, established the principle of civilian supremacy in military affairs, personally recruited his senior officer corps, and kept the states focused on a common goal.[[280]](#cite_note-l3gHY-312) Washington initially employed the inexperienced officers and untrained troops in [Fabian strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy "Fabian strategy") rather than risk frontal assaults against Britain's professional forces.[[281]](#cite_note-UxzJ5-313) Over the course of the war, Washington lost more battles than he won, but he never surrendered his troops and maintained a fighting force in the face of British field armies.[[282]](#cite_note-oBjRC-314)
552|
553|By prevailing European standards, the armies in America were relatively small, limited by lack of supplies and logistics. The British were constrained by the logistical difficulty of transporting troops across the Atlantic and their dependence on local supplies. Washington never directly commanded more than 17,000 men,[[283]](#cite_note-6Djag-315) and the combined Franco-American army in the decisive American victory at [Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Yorktown "Battle of Yorktown") was only about 19,000.[[284]](#cite_note-mtUen-316) At the beginning of 1776, Patriot forces consisted of 20,000 men, with two-thirds in the Continental Army and the other third in the state militias. About 250,000 American men served as regulars or as militia for the revolutionary cause during the war, but there were never more than 90,000 men under arms at any time.[[285]](#cite_note-0HyhO-317)
554|
555|On the whole, American officers never equaled their British opponents in tactics and maneuvers, and they lost most of the pitched battles. The great successes at Boston (1776), Saratoga (1777), and [Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown "Siege of Yorktown") (1781) were won by trapping the British far from base with a greater number of troops.[[277]](#cite_note-pSJBj-308) After 1778, Washington's army was transformed into a more disciplined and effective force, mostly as a product of [Baron von Steuben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_von_Steuben "Baron von Steuben")'s military training.[[276]](#cite_note-4DbAi-307) Immediately after the Continental Army emerged from Valley Forge in June 1778, it proved its ability to match the military capabilities of the British at the Battle of Monmouth, including a Black [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Rhode_Island_and_Providence_Plantations "Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations") regiment fending off a British bayonet attack and then counter charging the British for the first time as part of Washington's army.[[286]](#cite_note-kgNGc-318) After the Battle of Monmouth, Washington came to realize that saving entire towns was not necessary, but preserving his army and keeping the revolutionary spirit alive was more important. Washington informed [Henry Laurens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Laurens "Henry Laurens"), then president of the Second Continental Congress,[[ag]](#cite_note-320) "that the possession of our towns, while we have an army in the field, will avail them little."[[288]](#cite_note-76ZOZ-321)
556|
557|Although the Continental Congress was responsible for the war effort and provided supplies to the troops, Washington took it upon himself to pressure Congress and the state legislatures to provide the essentials of war; there was never nearly enough.[[289]](#cite_note-CX4G4-322) Congress evolved in its committee oversight and established the Board of War, which included members of the military.[[290]](#cite_note-rBEkF-323) Because the Board of War was also a committee ensnared with its own internal procedures, Congress also created the post of [Secretary of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War "United States Secretary of War"), appointing Major General Benjamin Lincoln to the position in February 1781. Washington worked closely with Lincoln to coordinate civilian and military authorities and took charge of training and supplying the army.[[291]](#cite_note-t1m52-324)[[276]](#cite_note-4DbAi-307)
558|
559|#### Continental Navy
560|
561|Main articles: [Continental Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Navy "Continental Navy") and [Continental Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Marines "Continental Marines")
562|
563|See also: [Privateer § American\_Revolutionary\_War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privateer#American_Revolutionary_War "Privateer"), and [Whaleboat War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaleboat_War "Whaleboat War")
564|
565|Further information: [Naval battles of the American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_battles_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Naval battles of the American Revolutionary War")
566|
567|[![ Sail warships at sea with full sail; in the center middle ground, the US ship; in the background, four French warships in a haze giving it a cannon salute with gunpowder; small boats also in the water in the middle ground.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/First_Recognition_of_the_American_Flag_by_a_Foreign_Government.jpg/250px-First_Recognition_of_the_American_Flag_by_a_Foreign_Government.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Recognition_of_the_American_Flag_by_a_Foreign_Government.jpg)
568|
569|[USS *Ranger*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Ranger_(1777) "USS Ranger (1777)") commanded by Captain [John Paul Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Paul_Jones "John Paul Jones")
570|
571|During the first summer of the war, Washington began outfitting schooners and other small seagoing vessels to prey on ships supplying the British in Boston.[[292]](#cite_note-N26y3-325) The Second Continental Congress established the Continental Navy on October 13, 1775, and appointed [Esek Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esek_Hopkins "Esek Hopkins") as its first commander;[[293]](#cite_note-ofLtd-326) for most of the war, the Continental Navy included only a handful of small frigates and sloops, supported by privateers.[[294]](#cite_note-o5APS-327) On November 10, 1775, Congress authorized the creation of the [Continental Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Marines "Continental Marines"), which ultimately evolved into the [United States Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps").[[279]](#cite_note-ztc3C-310)
572|
573|John Paul Jones became the first American naval hero when he captured [HMS *Drake*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Drake_(1777) "HMS Drake (1777)") on April 24, 1778, the first victory for any American military vessel in British waters.[[295]](#cite_note-L9ds0-328) The last such victory was by the frigate [USS *Alliance*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Alliance_(1778) "USS Alliance (1778)"), commanded by Captain [John Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Barry_(naval_officer) "John Barry (naval officer)"). On March 10, 1783, the *Alliance* outgunned HMS *Sybil* in a 45-minute duel while escorting Spanish gold from Havana to the Congress in Philadelphia.[[296]](#cite_note-unG7V-329) After Yorktown, all US Navy ships were sold or given away; it was the first time in America's history that it had no fighting forces on the high seas.[[297]](#cite_note-jC7za-330)
574|
575|Congress primarily commissioned privateers to reduce costs and to take advantage of the large proportion of colonial sailors found in the British Empire. In total, they included 1,700 ships that successfully captured 2,283 enemy ships to damage the British effort and to enrich themselves with the proceeds from the sale of cargo and the ship itself.[[298]](#cite_note-OVxVT-331)[[ah]](#cite_note-333) About 55,000 sailors served aboard American privateers during the war.[[15]](#cite_note-usmm-27)
576|
577|### France
578|
579|Main article: [France in the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_American_Revolution "France in the American Revolution")
580|
581|Further information: [History of the French Navy § Louis XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_French_Navy#Louis_XVI "History of the French Navy"), and [Military history of France § Ancien Régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_history_of_France#Ancien_Régime "Military history of France")
582|
583|At the beginning of the war, the Americans had no major international allies, since most nation-states waited to see how the conflict unfolded. Over time, the Continental Army established its military credibility. Battles such as the Battle of Bennington, the Battles of Saratoga, and even defeats such as the Battle of Germantown, proved decisive in gaining the support of powerful European nations, including France, Spain, and the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Anglo-Dutch_War#Background "Fourth Anglo-Dutch War"); the Dutch moved from covertly supplying the Americans with weapons and supplies to overtly supporting them.[[300]](#cite_note-zaqGl-334)
584|
585|The decisive American victory at Saratoga convinced [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_American_Revolutionary_War "France in the American Revolutionary War"), which was already a long-time rival of Britain, to offer the Americans the Treaty of Amity and Commerce. The two nations also agreed to a defensive Treaty of Alliance to protect their trade and also guaranteed American independence from Britain. To engage the United States as a French ally militarily, the treaty was conditioned on Britain initiating a war on France to stop it from trading with the US. Spain and the Dutch Republic were invited to join by both France and the United States in the treaty, but neither was responsive to the request.[[301]](#cite_note-yOYGS-335)
586|
587|On June 13, 1778, France declared war on Great Britain, and it invoked the French military alliance with the US, which ensured additional US private support for French possessions in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean").[[ai]](#cite_note-338) Washington worked closely with the soldiers and navy that France would send to America, primarily through Lafayette on his staff. French assistance made critical contributions required to defeat Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781.[[304]](#cite_note-fNRxX-339)[[aj]](#cite_note-341)
588|
589|### British strategy
590|
591|Further information: [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War")
592|
593|The British military had considerable experience fighting in North America.[[306]](#cite_note-cdOwo-342) However, in previous conflicts they benefited from local logistics and support from the colonial militia. In the American Revolutionary War, reinforcements had to come from Europe, and maintaining large armies over such distances was extremely complex; ships could take three months to cross the Atlantic, and orders from London were often outdated by the time they arrived.[[307]](#cite_note-HZaQ9-343)
594|
595|Prior to the conflict, the colonies were largely autonomous economic and political entities, with no centralized area of ultimate strategic importance.[[308]](#cite_note-Jvdgy-344) This meant that, unlike Europe where the fall of a capital city often ended wars, that in America continued even after the loss of major settlements such as Philadelphia, the seat of Congress, New York, and Charleston.[[309]](#cite_note-WTNUb-345) British power was reliant on the Royal Navy, whose dominance allowed them to resupply their own expeditionary forces while preventing access to enemy ports. However, the majority of the American population was agrarian, rather than urban; supported by the French navy and blockade runners based in the [Dutch Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Caribbean "Dutch Caribbean"), their economy was able to survive.[[310]](#cite_note-Pole_2004-346) [Lord North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_North,_2nd_Earl_of_Guilford "Frederick North, 2nd Earl of Guilford"), Prime Minister since 1770, delegated control of the war in North America to [Lord George Germain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_George_Germain "Lord George Germain") and the [Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Montagu,_4th_Earl_of_Sandwich "John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich"), who was [head of the Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lord_of_the_Admiralty "First Lord of the Admiralty") from 1771 to 1782. Defeat at Saratoga in 1777 made it clear the revolt would not be easily suppressed, especially after the Franco-American alliance of February 1778. With Spain also expected to join the conflict, the Royal Navy needed to prioritize either the war in America or in Europe; Germain advocated the former, Sandwich the latter.[[311]](#cite_note-Zfq4g-347)
596|
597|North initially backed the Southern strategy attempting to exploit divisions between the mercantile north and slave-owning south, but after the defeat of Yorktown, he was forced to accept that this policy had failed.[[312]](#cite_note-6mBg1-348) It was clear the war was lost, although the Royal Navy forced the French to relocate their fleet to the Caribbean in November 1781 and resumed a close blockade of American trade.[[313]](#cite_note-EiC1K-349) The resulting economic damage and rising inflation meant the US was now eager to end the war, while France was unable to provide further loans; Congress could no longer pay its soldiers.[[314]](#cite_note-q5EIL-350) The geographical size of the colonies and limited manpower meant the British could not simultaneously conduct military operations and occupy territory without local support. Debate persists over whether their defeat was inevitable; one British statesman described it as "like trying to conquer a map".[[315]](#cite_note-arzue-351) While [Ferling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_E._Ferling "John E. Ferling") argues Patriot victory was nothing short of a miracle,[[316]](#cite_note-holEy-352) [Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Ellis "Joseph Ellis") suggests the odds always favored the Americans, especially after Howe squandered the chance of a decisive British success in 1776, an "opportunity that would never come again".[[317]](#cite_note-MqYnj-353) The US military history speculates the additional commitment of 10,000 fresh troops in 1780 would have placed British victory "within the realm of possibility".[[318]](#cite_note-Ma3JT-354)
598|
599|#### British Army
600|
601|Main article: [British Army during the American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army_during_the_American_Revolutionary_War "British Army during the American Revolutionary War")
602|
603|See also: [Loyalist (American Revolution) § Military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution)#Military_service "Loyalist (American Revolution)")
604|
605|[![Portrait of the British commander-in-chief, Sir Thomas Gage in dress uniform.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Thomas_Gage_John_Singleton_Copley.jpeg/250px-Thomas_Gage_John_Singleton_Copley.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Gage_John_Singleton_Copley.jpeg)
606|
607|Sir [Thomas Gage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gage "Thomas Gage"), [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") Commander from 1763 to 1775
608|
609|The expulsion of France from North America in 1763 led to a drastic reduction in British troop levels in the colonies; in 1775, there were only 8,500 regular soldiers among a civilian population of 2.8 million.[[319]](#cite_note-0qbek-355) The bulk of military resources in the Americas were focused on defending sugar islands in the Caribbean; [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Jamaica "Colony of Jamaica") alone generated more revenue than all thirteen American colonies combined.[[320]](#cite_note-FJWrp-356) With the end of the Seven Years' War, the permanent army in Britain was also cut back, which resulted in administrative difficulties when the war began a decade later.[[321]](#cite_note-Y118y-357)
610|
611|Over the course of the war, there were four separate British commanders-in-chief. The first was Thomas Gage, appointed in 1763, whose initial focus was establishing British rule in former French areas of Canada. Many in London blamed the revolt on his failure to take firm action earlier, and he was relieved after the heavy losses incurred at the Battle of Bunker Hill.[[322]](#cite_note-cosou-358) His replacement was Sir William Howe, a member of the Whig faction in Parliament who opposed the policy of coercion advocated by Lord North; Cornwallis, who later surrendered at Yorktown, was one of many senior officers who initially refused to serve in North America.[[323]](#cite_note-CZWL2-359)
612|
613|The 1775 campaign showed the British overestimated the capabilities of their own troops and underestimated the colonial militia, requiring a reassessment of tactics and strategy,[[324]](#cite_note-pWpln-360) and allowing the Patriots to take the initiative.[[325]](#cite_note-57mVs-361) Howe's responsibility is still debated; despite receiving large numbers of reinforcements, Bunker Hill seems to have permanently affected his self-confidence and lack of tactical flexibility meant he often failed to follow up opportunities.[[326]](#cite_note-r4hyC-362) Many of his decisions were attributed to supply problems, such as his failure to pursue Washington's beaten army.[[327]](#cite_note-MlUcq-363) Having lost the confidence of his subordinates, he was recalled after Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga.[[328]](#cite_note-UkMe5-364)
614|
615|Following the failure of the Carlisle Commission, British policy changed from treating the Patriots as subjects who needed to be reconciled to enemies who had to be defeated.[[329]](#cite_note-o6DjZ-365) In 1778, Howe was replaced by Sir Henry Clinton.[[330]](#cite_note-eA9wm-366) Regarded as an expert on tactics and strategy,[[328]](#cite_note-UkMe5-364) like his predecessors Clinton was handicapped by chronic supply issues.[[331]](#cite_note-BZg2c-367) In addition, Clinton's strategy was compromised by conflict with political superiors in London and his colleagues in North America, especially Admiral [Mariot Arbuthnot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariot_Arbuthnot "Mariot Arbuthnot"), replaced in early 1781 by Rodney.[[250]](#cite_note-ap5wX-280) He was neither notified nor consulted when Germain approved Cornwallis's invasion of the south in 1781 and delayed sending him reinforcements believing the bulk of Washington's army was still outside New York City.[[332]](#cite_note-mWJRm-368) After the surrender at Yorktown, Clinton was relieved by Carleton, whose major task was to oversee the evacuation of Loyalists and British troops from Savannah, Charleston, and New York City.[[333]](#cite_note-YZsHH-369)
616|
617|#### German troops
618|
619|Main article: [Hessian (soldier)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hessian_(soldier) "Hessian (soldier)")
620|
621|[![Hessian troops surrender after Battle of Trenton, December 1776](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Surrender_of_the_Hessian_Troops_to_General_Washington%2C_after_The_Battle_of_Trenton._December_1776._Copy_of_lithograph%2C_1_-_NARA_-_532880.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Surrender_of_the_Hessian_Troops_to_General_Washington%2C_after_The_Battle_of_Trenton._December_1776._Copy_of_lithograph%2C_1_-_NARA_-_532880.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Surrender_of_the_Hessian_Troops_to_General_Washington,_after_The_Battle_of_Trenton._December_1776._Copy_of_lithograph,_1_-_NARA_-_532880.tif)
622|
623|[Hessian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hessian_(soldier) "Hessian (soldier)") troops surrender after [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington")'s victory at the [Battle of Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trenton "Battle of Trenton") in December 1776
624|
625|During the 18th century, states commonly [hired foreign soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldatenhandel "Soldatenhandel"), including Britain.[[334]](#cite_note-jSAGZ-370) When it became clear additional troops were needed to suppress the revolt in America, it was decided to employ [professional German soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans_in_the_American_Revolution#Allies_of_Great_Britain "Germans in the American Revolution"). There were several reasons for this, including public sympathy for the Patriot cause, a historical reluctance to expand the British army and the time needed to recruit and train new regiments.[[335]](#cite_note-cCTlC-371) Many smaller states in the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") had a long tradition of renting their armies to the highest bidder. The most important was [Hesse-Kassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landgraviate_of_Hesse-Kassel "Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel"), known as "the Mercenary State".[[336]](#cite_note-NNZE8-372)
626|
627|The first supply agreements were signed by the North administration in late 1775; 30,000 Germans served in the American War.[[337]](#cite_note-btSGH-373) Often generically referred to as "Hessians", they included men from many other states, including [Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoverian_Army "Hanoverian Army") and [Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electorate_of_Brunswick-Lüneburg "Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg").[[338]](#cite_note-srbv4-374) Sir Henry Clinton recommended recruiting Russian troops whom he rated very highly, having seen them in action against the [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1768–1774) "Russo-Turkish War (1768–1774)"); however, negotiations with [Catherine the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_the_Great "Catherine the Great") made little progress.[[339]](#cite_note-IqLsU-375)
628|
629|Unlike previous wars their use led to intense political debate in Britain, France, and even Germany, where [Frederick the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_the_Great "Frederick the Great") refused to provide passage through his territories for troops hired for the American war.[[340]](#cite_note-schmidt208-209-376) In March 1776, the agreements were challenged in Parliament by Whigs who objected to "coercion" in general, and the use of foreign soldiers to subdue "British subjects".[[341]](#cite_note-vyLv6-377) The debates were covered in detail by American newspapers; in May 1776 they received copies of the treaties themselves, provided by British sympathizers and smuggled into North America from London.[[342]](#cite_note-tIwST-378)
630|
631|The prospect of foreign German soldiers being used in the colonies bolstered support for independence, more so than taxation and other acts combined; the King was accused of declaring war on his own subjects, leading to the idea there were now two separate governments.[[343]](#cite_note-ImWYT-379)[[344]](#cite_note-juHEN-380) By apparently showing Britain was determined to go to war, it made hopes of reconciliation seem naive and hopeless, while the employment of what was regarded as "foreign mercenaries" became one of the charges levelled against George III in the Declaration of Independence.[[340]](#cite_note-schmidt208-209-376) The Hessian reputation within Germany for brutality also increased support for the Patriot cause among German American immigrants.[[345]](#cite_note-taPBr-381)
632|
633|The presence of over 150,000 [German Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Americans "German Americans") meant both sides felt the German soldiers might be persuaded to desert; one reason Clinton suggested employing Russians was that he felt they were less likely to defect. When the first German troops arrived on Staten Island in August 1776, Congress approved the printing of handbills, promising land and citizenship to any willing to join the Patriot cause. The British launched a counter-campaign claiming deserters could be executed.[[346]](#cite_note-mauch415-382) Desertion among the Germans occurred throughout the war, with the highest rate of desertion occurring between the surrender at Yorktown and the Treaty of Paris.[[347]](#cite_note-Nf6u9-383) German regiments were central to the British war effort; of the estimated 30,000 sent to America, some 13,000 became casualties.[[348]](#cite_note-bnmql-384)
634|
635|## Revolution as civil war
636|
637|### Loyalists
638|
639|Main article: [Loyalist (American Revolution)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)")
640|
641|See also: [American Legion (Great Britain)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Legion_(Great_Britain) "American Legion (Great Britain)") and [Prince of Wales' American Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales'_American_Regiment "Prince of Wales' American Regiment")
642|
643|[![A wounded British officer falls from his horse after being struck by gunfire; another British officer to his rights puts his hands forwards to support the wounded rider; troops skirmish in the background; men lie dead at the riders feet.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/KingsMountain_DeathOfFerguson_Chappel.jpg/250px-KingsMountain_DeathOfFerguson_Chappel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KingsMountain_DeathOfFerguson_Chappel.jpg)
644|
645|American [Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) "Patriot (American Revolution)") routed [Loyalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)") at the [Battle of Kings Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kings_Mountain "Battle of Kings Mountain") in 1780, raising Patriot morale.
646|
647|Wealthy Loyalists convinced the British government that most of the colonists were sympathetic toward the Crown;[[349]](#cite_note-6cWCe-385) consequently, British military planners relied on recruiting Loyalists, but had trouble recruiting sufficient numbers as the Patriots had widespread support.[[275]](#cite_note-JOPiQ-306)[[ak]](#cite_note-386) Approximately 25,000 Loyalists fought for the British throughout the war.[[30]](#cite_note-savas41-49) Although Loyalists constituted about twenty percent of the colonial population,[[81]](#cite_note-Greene_p._235-104) they were concentrated in distinct communities. Many of them lived among large plantation owners in the [Tidewater region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidewater_(region) "Tidewater (region)") and [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_in_the_American_Revolution#Early_conflicts "South Carolina in the American Revolution").[[81]](#cite_note-Greene_p._235-104)
648|
649|When the British began probing the backcountry in 1777–1778, they were faced with a major problem: any significant level of organized Loyalist activity required a continued presence of British regulars.[[350]](#cite_note-Gu69t-387) The available manpower that the British had in America was insufficient to protect Loyalist territory and counter American offensives.[[351]](#cite_note-xeYC7-388) The Loyalist militias in the South were constantly defeated by neighboring Patriot militia. The Patriot victory at the Battle of Kings Mountain irreversibly impaired Loyalist militia capability in the South.[[231]](#cite_note-NcMDc-258)
650|
651|When the early war policy was administered by Howe, the Crown's need to maintain Loyalist support prevented it from using the traditional revolt suppression methods.[[352]](#cite_note-m4e3v-389) The British cause suffered when their troops ransacked local homes during an aborted attack on Charleston in 1779 that enraged both Patriots and Loyalists.[[219]](#cite_note-yBaSD-246) After Congress rejected the [Carlisle Peace Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle_Peace_Commission "Carlisle Peace Commission") in 1778 and Westminster turned to "hard war" during Clinton's command, neutral colonists in the Carolinas often allied with the Patriots.[[353]](#cite_note-dh9oI-390) Conversely, Loyalists gained support when Patriots intimidated suspected Tories by destroying property or [tarring and feathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarring_and_feathering "Tarring and feathering").[[354]](#cite_note-4VC7B-391)
652|
653|A Loyalist militia unit—the [British Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Legion_(American_Revolutionary_War) "British Legion (American Revolutionary War)")—provided some of the best troops in British service.[[355]](#cite_note-b5poP-392) It was commanded by Tarleton and gained a fearsome reputation in the colonies for "brutality and needless slaughter".[[356]](#cite_note-rankin-393)[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*]
654|
655|### Women
656|
657|Main article: [Women in the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_American_Revolution "Women in the American Revolution")
658|
659|[![Scene of Nancy Morgan Hart on the left with musket raised and child hiding behind her skirts, and behind; on the right two Loyalist soldiers are lying on the floor, and three are raising their hands defensively in alarm.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Nancy_Morgan_Hart.gif/250px-Nancy_Morgan_Hart.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nancy_Morgan_Hart.gif)
660|
661|[Nancy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Hart "Nancy Hart") single-handedly captured six [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)") soldiers who barged into her home intending to ransack it.
662|
663|Women played various roles during the Revolutionary War; they often accompanied their husbands when permitted. For example, throughout the war [Martha Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Washington "Martha Washington") was known to visit and provide aid to her husband George at various American camps.[[357]](#cite_note-NsXgO-394) Women often accompanied armies as [camp followers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_follower "Camp follower") to sell goods and perform necessary tasks in hospitals and camps, and numbered in the thousands during the war.[[358]](#cite_note-s5toN-395)
664|
665|Women also assumed military roles: some dressed as men to directly support combat, fight, or act as spies on both sides.[[359]](#cite_note-HUZJR-396) Anna Maria Lane joined her husband in the Army. The Virginia General Assembly later cited her bravery: she fought while dressed as a man and "performed extraordinary military services, and received a severe wound at the battle of Germantown ... with the courage of a soldier".[[360]](#cite_note-F5oSv-397) On April 26, 1777, [Sybil Ludington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sybil_Ludington "Sybil Ludington") is said to have ridden to alert militia forces to the British's approach; she has been called the "female Paul Revere".[[361]](#cite_note-om7F0-398) Whether the ride occurred is questioned.[[362]](#cite_note-Hunt-399)[[363]](#cite_note-Tucker-400)[[364]](#cite_note-Lewis-401)[[365]](#cite_note-Eschner-402) A few others [disguised themselves as men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wartime_cross-dressers "List of wartime cross-dressers"). [Deborah Sampson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Sampson "Deborah Sampson") fought until her gender was discovered and she was discharged as a result; [Sally St. Clair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_St._Clair "Sally St. Clair") was killed in action.[[360]](#cite_note-F5oSv-397)
666|
667|### African Americans
668|
669|Main article: [African Americans in the Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans_in_the_Revolutionary_War "African Americans in the Revolutionary War")
670|
671|[![A scene of four uniformed soldiers of the Continental 1st Rhode Island Regiment. On the left, a black and a white soldier formally at ](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Soldiers_at_the_siege_of_Yorktown_%281781%29%2C_by_Jean-Baptiste-Antoine_DeVerger_%28cropped1%29.png/250px-Soldiers_at_the_siege_of_Yorktown_%281781%29%2C_by_Jean-Baptiste-Antoine_DeVerger_%28cropped1%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Soldiers_at_the_siege_of_Yorktown_(1781),_by_Jean-Baptiste-Antoine_DeVerger_(cropped1).png)
672|
673|[Continental Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army") soldiers, including one from the [1st Rhode Island Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Rhode_Island_Regiment "1st Rhode Island Regiment") on the left
674|
675|When war began, the population of the Thirteen Colonies included an estimated 500,000 slaves, predominantly used as labor on [Southern plantations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation_complexes_in_the_Southern_United_States "Plantation complexes in the Southern United States").[[366]](#cite_note-517PM-403) In November 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, issued a proclamation that promised freedom to any Patriot-owned slaves willing to bear arms. Although the announcement helped to fill a temporary manpower shortage, white Loyalist prejudice meant recruits were eventually redirected to non-combatant roles. The Loyalists' motive was to deprive Patriot [planters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planter_class "Planter class") of labor rather than to end slavery; Loyalist-owned slaves were returned.[[367]](#cite_note-CJ6XK-404)
676|
677|The 1779 [Philipsburg Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipsburg_Proclamation "Philipsburg Proclamation") issued by Clinton extended the offer of freedom to Patriot-owned slaves throughout the colonies. It persuaded entire families to escape to British lines, many of which were employed growing food for the army by removing the requirement for military service. While Clinton organized the [Black Pioneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Pioneers "Black Pioneers"), he also ensured fugitive slaves were returned to Loyalist owners with orders that they were not to be punished.[[368]](#cite_note-DKDsq-405) As the war progressed, service as regular soldiers in British units became increasingly common; Black Loyalists formed two regiments of the Charleston garrison in 1783.[[369]](#cite_note-bfNHp-406)
678|
679|Estimates of the numbers who served the British during the war vary from 25,000 to 50,000, excluding those who escaped during wartime. Thomas Jefferson estimated that Virginia may have lost 30,000 slaves to escapes.[[370]](#cite_note-zag2G-407) In South Carolina, nearly 25,000 slaves (about 30 percent of the enslaved population) either fled, migrated, or died, which significantly disrupted the plantation economies both during and after the war.[[371]](#cite_note-yRG5O-408)
680|
681|[Black Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Patriot "Black Patriot") were barred from the Continental Army until Washington convinced Congress in January 1778 that there was no other way to replace losses from disease and desertion. The [1st Rhode Island Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Rhode_Island_Regiment "1st Rhode Island Regiment") formed in February included former slaves whose owners were compensated; however, only 140 of its 225 soldiers were Black and recruitment stopped in June 1788.[[372]](#cite_note-Ltvqf-409) Ultimately, around 5,000 African Americans served in the Continental Army and Navy in a variety of roles, while another 4,000 were employed in Patriot militia units, aboard privateers, or as teamsters, servants, and spies. After the war, a small minority received land grants or Congressional pensions; many others were returned to their masters post-war despite earlier promises of freedom.[[373]](#cite_note-aJJzP-410)
682|
683|As a Patriot victory became increasingly likely, the treatment of Black Loyalists became a point of contention; after the surrender of Yorktown in 1781, Washington insisted all escapees be returned but Cornwallis refused. In 1782 and 1783, around 8,000 to 10,000 freed Blacks were evacuated by the British from Charleston, Savannah, and New York; some moved onto London, while 3,000 to 4,000 settled in Nova Scotia.[[374]](#cite_note-Bvc5o-411) White Loyalists transported 15,000 enslaved Blacks to Jamaica and the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"). The free Black Loyalists who migrated to the British West Indies included regular soldiers from Dunmore's [Ethiopian Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Regiment "Ethiopian Regiment"), and those from Charleston who helped garrison the [Leeward Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeward_Islands "Leeward Islands").[[369]](#cite_note-bfNHp-406)
684|
685|### Native Americans
686|
687|Main page: [Category:Native American people in the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Native_American_people_in_the_American_Revolution "Category:Native American people in the American Revolution")
688|
689|Further information: [Western theater of the American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_theater_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Western theater of the American Revolutionary War"), [Northern theater of the American Revolutionary War after Saratoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_theater_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War_after_Saratoga "Northern theater of the American Revolutionary War after Saratoga"), [Brodhead's Coshocton expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brodhead's_Coshocton_expedition "Brodhead's Coshocton expedition"), and [Gnadenhutten massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnadenhutten_massacre "Gnadenhutten massacre")
690|
691|[![Portrait of British regular army Colonel Joseph Brant, Iroquois Mohawk.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Joseph_Brant_2.jpg/250px-Joseph_Brant_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Brant_2.jpg)
692|
693|Colonel [Joseph Brant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Brant "Joseph Brant") of the British-led [Mohawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohawk_people#American_Revolutionary_War "Mohawk people") in the war
694|
695|Most Native Americans east of the Mississippi River were affected by the war, and many tribes were divided over how to respond. A few tribes were friendly with the colonists, but most Natives opposed the union of the Colonies as a potential threat to their territory. Approximately 13,000 Natives fought on the British side, with the largest group coming from tribal factions of the [Haudenosaunee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_Confederacy "Haudenosaunee Confederacy") (*also* Iroquois) who deployed around 1,500 men.[[32]](#cite_note-Greene_p._393-52)
696|
697|Early in July 1776, [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee") allies of Britain attacked the short-lived [Washington District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_District,_North_Carolina "Washington District, North Carolina") of [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Colony "North Carolina Colony"). Their defeat splintered both Cherokee settlements and people, and was directly responsible for the rise of the [Chickamauga Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickamauga_Cherokee "Chickamauga Cherokee"), who perpetrated the [Cherokee–American wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee–American_wars "Cherokee–American wars") against American settlers for decades after hostilities with Britain ended.[[375]](#cite_note-finger2001-412)
698|
699|[Muscogee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee "Muscogee") and other allies of Britain fought against Americans in Georgia and South Carolina. In 1778, a force of 800 Muscogee destroyed American settlements along the [Broad River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_River_(Georgia) "Broad River (Georgia)") in Georgia. Muscogee warriors also joined [Thomas Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Brown_(loyalist) "Thomas Brown (loyalist)")'s raids into South Carolina and assisted Britain during the siege of Savannah.[[376]](#cite_note-KPNF9-413) Many Native Americans were involved in the fight between Britain and Spain on the Gulf Coast and along the British side of the Mississippi River. Thousands of Muscogee, [Chickasaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickasaw "Chickasaw"), and [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") fought in major battles such as the [Battle of Fort Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Charlotte "Battle of Fort Charlotte"), the [Battle of Mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mobile_(1781) "Battle of Mobile (1781)"), and the [siege of Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Pensacola "Siege of Pensacola").[[377]](#cite_note-npQH7-414)

233|The **American Revolutionary War** (April 19, 1775 – September 3, 1783), also known as the **Revolutionary War** or **American War of Independence** or simply the **American Revolution**, was the armed conflict that comprised the final eight years of the broader [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"), in which American [Patriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) "Patriot (American Revolution)") forces organized as the [Continental Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army") and, commanded by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington"), defeated the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army_during_the_American_Revolutionary_War "British Army during the American Revolutionary War"). The conflict was fought in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), and the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"). The war's outcome seemed uncertain for most of the war, but Washington and the Continental Army's decisive victory in the [Siege of Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown "Siege of Yorktown") in 1781 led King [George III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_III "George III") and the [Kingdom of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") to negotiate an end to the war. In 1783, in the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)"), the British monarchy acknowledged the independence of the [Thirteen Colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"), leading to the establishment of the United States as an independent and sovereign nation.
234|
235|In 1763, after the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") gained dominance in North America following its victory over the French in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), tensions and disputes began escalating between the British and the Thirteen Colonies, especially following passage of the [Stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_1765 "Stamp Act 1765") and [Townshend Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townshend_Acts "Townshend Acts"). The British Army responded by seeking to occupy [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") militarily, leading to the [Boston Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Massacre "Boston Massacre") on March 5, 1770. In mid-1774, with tensions escalating even further between the British Army and the colonies, the British Parliament imposed the [Intolerable Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intolerable_Acts "Intolerable Acts"), an attempt to disarm Americans, leading to the [Battles of Lexington and Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord "Battles of Lexington and Concord") in April 1775, the first battles of the Revolutionary War. In June 1775, the [Second Continental Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Continental_Congress "Second Continental Congress") voted to incorporate colonial-based Patriot militias into a central military, the Continental Army, and unanimously appointed Washington its commander-in-chief. Two months later, in August 1775, [George III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_III "George III") [declared the colonies to be in a state of rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_Rebellion "Proclamation of Rebellion"). In July 1776, the Second Continental Congress formalized the war, passing the [Lee Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Resolution "Lee Resolution") on July 2, and, two days later, unanimously adopting the [Declaration o... [truncated]
236|
237|In March 1776, in an early win for the newly-formed Continental Army under Washington's command, following a [successful siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Boston "Siege of Boston") of Boston, the Continental Army successfully drove the British Army out of Boston. British commander in chief [William Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Howe,_5th_Viscount_Howe "William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe") responded by launching the [New York and New Jersey campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_and_New_Jersey_campaign "New York and New Jersey campaign"), which resulted in Howe's capture of New York City in November. Washington responded by [clandestinely crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington's_crossing_of_the_Delaware_River "George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River") the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") and winning small but significant victories at [Trenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trenton "Battle of Trenton") and [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Princeton "Battle of Princeton").
238|
239|In the summer of 1777, as Howe was poised to [capture Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_campaign "Philadelphia campaign"), the Continental Congress fled to [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"). In October 1777, a separate northern British force under the command of [John Burgoyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Burgoyne "John Burgoyne") was forced to surrender at [Saratoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Saratoga "Battles of Saratoga") in an American victory that proved crucial in convincing France and Spain that an independent United States was a viable possibility. France signed a [commercial agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce_(France–United_States) "Treaty of Amity and Commerce (France–United States)") with the revolutionaries, followed by a [Treaty of Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Alliance_(1778) "Treaty of Alliance (1778)") in February 1778. In 1779, the [Sullivan Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Expedition "Sullivan Expedition") undertook a [scorched earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorched_earth "Scorched earth") campaign against British-allied [factions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_faction "Political faction") of the [Haudenosaunee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_Confederacy "Haudenosaunee Confederacy") (*also* Iroquois). [Native American raids on the American frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_theater_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Western theater of the American Revolutionary War"), however, continued to be a problem. Also, in 1779, Spain allied with France against Great Britain in the [Treaty of Aranjuez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Aranjuez_(1779) "Treaty of Aranjuez (1779)"), though Spain did not formally ally with the Americans.
240|
241|Howe's replacement [Henry Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clinton_(British_Army_officer,_born_1730) "Henry Clinton (British Army officer, born 1730)") intended to take the war against the Americans into the [Southern Colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Colonies "Southern Colonies"). Despite some initial success, British General [Cornwallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Cornwallis,_1st_Marquess_Cornwallis "Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis") was besieged by a Franco-American army in [Yorktown, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown_(1781) "Siege of Yorktown (1781)"), in September and October 1781. The [French navy cut off Cornwallis's escape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Chesapeake "Battle of the Chesapeake") and he was forced to surrender in October. The British wars with France and Spain continued for another two years, but fighting largely ceased in North America. In the Treaty of Paris, signed on September 3, 1783, Great Britain acknowledged the sovereignty and independence of the United States, bringing the American Revolutionary War to an end. The [Treaties of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Paris_(1783) "Peace of Paris (1783)") resolved Great Britain's conflicts with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-French_War_(1778–1783) "Anglo-French War (1778–1783)") and [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Spain and the American Revolutionary War"), and forced Great Britain to cede [Tobago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobago "Tobago"), [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_capture_of_Senegal "British capture of Senegal"), and small territories in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_India "French India") to France, and [Menorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Minorca_(1781) "Invasion of Minorca (1781)"), [West Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Florida "West Florida"), and [East Flor... 253|The French and Indian War, part of the wider global conflict known as the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), ended with the [1763 Peace of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Paris_(1763) "Peace of Paris (1763)"), which expelled [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire "French colonial empire") from their possessions in [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France").[[45]](#cite_note-wtW8l-67) The [Royal Proclamation of 1763](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Proclamation_of_1763 "Royal Proclamation of 1763") was designed to refocus colonial expansion north into [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") and south into [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), with the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") as the dividing line between British and [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") possessions in America. Settlement was tightly restricted beyond the 1763 limits, and claims west of this line, including by [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia") and [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Massachusetts_Bay "Province of Massachusetts Bay"), were rescinded.[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELass19803-68) With the exception of Virginia and others deprived of rights to western lands, the [colonial legislatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_government_in_the_Thirteen_Colonies "Colonial government in the Thirteen Colonies") agreed on the boundaries but disagreed on where to set them. Many settlers resented the restrictions entirely, and enforcement required permanent garrisons along the frontier, which led to increasingly bitter disputes over who should pay for them.[[47]](#cite_note-pb2Zp-69)

263|The huge debt incurred by the Seven Years' War and demands from British taxpayers for cuts in government expenditure meant [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain "Parliament of Great Britain") expected the colonies to fund their own defense.[[47]](#cite_note-pb2Zp-69) The 1763 to 1765 [Grenville ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenville_ministry "Grenville ministry") instructed the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Royal_Navy_(after_1707) "History of the Royal Navy (after 1707)") to cease trading smuggled goods and enforce customs duties levied in American ports.[[47]](#cite_note-pb2Zp-69) The most important was the 1733 [Molasses Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molasses_Act "Molasses Act"); routinely ignored before 1763, it had a significant economic impact since 85% of New England rum exports were manufactured from imported molasses. These measures were followed by the [Sugar Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Act "Sugar Act") and [Stamp Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_(1765) "Stamp Act (1765)"), which imposed additional taxes on the colonies to pay for defending the western frontier.[[48]](#cite_note-4R8zt-70) The taxes proved highly burdensome, particularly for the poorer classes, and quickly became a source of discontent.[[49]](#cite_note-71) In July 1765, the [Whigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whigs_(British_political_party) "Whigs (British political party)") formed the [First Rockingham ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Rockingham_ministry "First Rockingham ministry"), which repealed the Stamp Act and reduced tax on foreign molasses to help the New England economy, but re-asserted Parliamentary authority in the [Declaratory Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaratory_Act "Declaratory Act").[[50]](#cite_note-Leqka-72)
264|
265|However, this did little to end the discontent; in 1768, a riot started in Boston when the authorities seized the sloop *[Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Liberty_(1768) "HMS Liberty (1768)")* on suspicion of smuggling.[[51]](#cite_note-sImY5-73) Tensions escalated in March 1770 when British troops fired on rock-throwing civilians, killing five in what became known as the [Boston Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Massacre "Boston Massacre").[[52]](#cite_note-kIDxS-74) The Massacre coincided with the partial repeal of the [Townshend Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townshend_Acts "Townshend Acts") by the Tory-based [North Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Ministry "North Ministry"). North insisted on retaining duty on tea to enshrine Parliament's right to tax the colonies; the amount was minor, but ignored the fact it was that very principle Americans found objectionable.[[53]](#cite_note-HdjZT-75)
266|
267|In April 1772, colonialists staged the first American tax revolt against British royal authority in [Weare, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weare,_New_Hampshire "Weare, New Hampshire"), later referred to as the [Pine Tree Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine_Tree_Riot "Pine Tree Riot").[[54]](#cite_note-76) This would inspire the design of the [Pine Tree Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine_Tree_Flag "Pine Tree Flag"). Tensions escalated following the destruction of a customs vessel in the June 1772 [Gaspee Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspee_Affair "Gaspee Affair"), then came to a head in 1773. A [banking crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_1772 "Crisis of 1772") led to the near-collapse of the [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company "East India Company"), which dominated the British economy; to support it, Parliament passed the [Tea Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Act "Tea Act"), giving it a trading monopoly in the [Thirteen Colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"). Since most American tea was smuggled by the Dutch, the act was opposed by those who managed the illegal trade, while being seen as another attempt to impose the principle of taxation by Parliament.[[55]](#cite_note-oTpsv-77) In December 1773, a group called the [Sons of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_Liberty "Sons of Liberty") disguised as [Mohawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohawk_people "Mohawk people") dumped crates of tea into [Boston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Harbor "Boston Harbor"), an event later known as the [Boston Tea Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Tea_Party "Boston Tea Party"). 269|### Break with the British Crown
270|
271|Further information: [Battles of Lexington and Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord "Battles of Lexington and Concord") and [First Continental Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Continental_Congress "First Continental Congress")
272|
273|Throughout the 18th century, the [elected lower houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_government_in_the_Thirteen_Colonies#Assembly "Colonial government in the Thirteen Colonies") in the colonial legislatures gradually wrested power from their governors.[[57]](#cite_note-0pRKw-79) Dominated by smaller landowners and merchants, these assemblies now established ad-hoc provincial legislatures, effectively replacing royal control. With the exception of [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Georgia "Province of Georgia"), twelve colonies sent representatives to the [First Continental Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Continental_Congress "First Continental Congress") to agree on a unified response to the crisis.[[58]](#cite_note-0j3B4-80) Many of the delegates feared that a boycott would result in war and sent a [Petition to the King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petition_to_the_King "Petition to the King") calling for the repeal of the Intolerable Acts.[[59]](#cite_note-BkMNP-81) After some debate, on September 17, 1774, Congress endorsed the Massachusetts [Suffolk Resolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffolk_Resolves "Suffolk Resolves") and on October 20 passed the [Continental Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Association "Continental Association"), which instituted [economic sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_sanctions "Economic sanctions") and a boycott of goods against Britain.[[60]](#cite_note-yBXBu-82)
274|
275|While denying its authority over internal American affairs, a faction led by [James Duane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Duane "James Duane") and future [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) "Loyalist (American Revolution)") [Joseph Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Galloway "Joseph Galloway") insisted Congress recognize Parliament's right to regulate colonial trade.[[60]](#cite_note-yBXBu-82)[[w]](#cite_note-83) Expecting concessions by the North administration, Congress authorized the colonial legislatures to enforce the boycott; this succeeded in reducing British imports by 97% from 1774 to 1775.[[61]](#cite_note-RVpda-84) However, on February 9 Parliament declared Massachusetts to be in rebellion and instituted a blockade of the colony.[[62]](#cite_note-X94UC-85) In July, the [Restraining Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restraining_Acts_1775 "Restraining Acts 1775") limited colonial trade with the [British West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_West_Indies "British West Indies") and Britain and barred New England ships from the [Newfoundland cod fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Newfoundland_and_Labrador#Fishing "History of Newfoundland and Labrador"). Based on authoritative U.S. government sources, here's the definitive comparison:

## Official Date: **September 3, 1783** (Treaty of Paris signing)

### Candidate Dates Compared

| Date | Event | Legal/Diplomatic Status |
|------|-------|-------------------------|
| **Oct 19, 1781** | Yorktown surrender | Decisive *military* victory making independence inevitable; did not legally establish it. British still held NYC, Charleston, Savannah. Fighting continued at sea and in other theaters for 2 more years. |
| **Sept 3, 1783** | **Treaty of Paris signed** | **Britain formally recognized U.S. independence** (Article 1). National Archives: "ended the American Revolution and formally recognized the United States as an independent nation." |
| **Jan 14, 1784** | U.S. Congress ratified | Domestic legal approval; LOC: "officially establishing the United States as an independent and sovereign nation." |
| **May 12, 1784** | Ratifications exchanged | Treaty fully effective under international law (per Article 10's 6-month window). |

### Authoritative Sources

1. **U.S. National Archives** (archives.gov): "This treaty, signed on September 3, 1783... ended the American Revolution and **formally recognized the United States as an independent nation**." — *Milestone Documents: Treaty of Paris (1783)*

2. **Library of Congress** (loc.gov): "The Continental Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris on January 14, 1784, **officially establishing the United States as an independent and sovereign nation**." — *Today in History: January 14*

3. **U.S. State Dept. Office of the Historian** (history.state.gov): "The war was **not officially concluded**... until the agreement to the Treaty of Paris in 1783... The final treaty **granted full independence** and recognized the borders of the new United States of America." — *Milestones: 1776–1783*

### Conclusion

**September 3, 1783** is the date American independence was officially *won* in the diplomatic/legal sense — when Great Britain explicitly acknowledged U.S. sovereignty in Article 1 of the signed treaty. Yorktown was the military turning point; the Treaty of Paris was the legal instrument. The January 14, 1784 congressional ratification completed the U.S. domestic constitutional process, and May 12, 1784 completed the international legal process.

# How many of the signers were born in the American Colonies?

48 of the 56 signers were born in America. Two were born in England (Button Gwinnett, Robert Morris), two in Ireland (George Taylor, Matthew Thornton), two in Scotland (James Wilson, John Witherspoon), one in Northern Ireland (James Smith), and one in Wales (Francis Lewis).
